These Technical Measures Warned of Stock Market Whiplash
 
Plus, the Trillion Dollar Man
 

Monday’s epic stock-market rebound is the second one tied to a single man in the past year-and-a-half. Last April it was President Trump softening his own “Liberation Day” tariffs. This time it was Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia. Based on stock futures, this bounce might not quite have the legs of last year’s rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite is set to open about 1% lower.

‘Nothing good happens’

 

Who could’ve seen it coming?

 

No, not Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia—all the crazy market volatility of the past few days. It didn’t quite rise to the level of something we’ll be telling our grandchildren about, but the face-ripping moves were extraordinary.

 

Whittle the historical list of market whipsaws down to times when there wasn’t some unexpected shock such as a terror attack, bank collapse, war or pandemic and it was extremely unusual.

 

Technical analysts weren’t completely blindsided, though, after one of their most widely followed indicators flashed a warning last week. “Nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average,” goes the saying.

 

The market spends about three-quarters of its time above that line, but analysts at Freedom Capital Markets point out that 17 of the 20 largest one-day drops since 1950 occurred when the S&P 500 was below it.

 

Stocks usually recover quickly. Analysts at LPL Financial say that, of almost 300 instances since 1928, the median time it took the index to go back above its 200-day moving average has been just four days.

 

But few of those rebounds are as powerful as what we saw Monday. Technical analysts weren’t so surprised by that either.

 

An even rarer technical indicator was triggered on Friday—a drop to four standard deviations below the index’s 50-day moving average. Analysts at Bespoke Investment Group dubbed it “apocalyptically oversold.”

 

Of only five similar instances going back to the 1960s, three were followed by very sharp bounces the next session. More interesting now that the initial rebound is over is that the S&P 500 rose every year following those oversold readings. The average gain was nearly 20%.

 

That sounds encouraging, but look closely at the dates in the chart below: Nov. 22, 1963 was the day JFK was shot. Oct. 19, 1987 was the Black Monday stock-market crash, Aug. 6, 1990 was after Iraq invaded Kuwait and Aug. 8, 2011 was when the U.S. lost its triple-A credit rating.

 

Those all made investors fearful about the future. The market had a steep wall of worry to climb as life got back to normal.

 

The only “apocalyptically oversold” reading caused by general market jitters—a slowing Chinese economy and falling oil prices in 2015—preceded the mildest one-year rebound.

 

The recent AI selloff seems more like that. There’s been a drip-drip-drip of concerning news the past few weeks rather than a single shock event. Underlying conditions were still good enough last week for Anthropic to complete the largest initial public offering in history.

 

Monday’s rebound was extraordinary, no doubt enhanced by Huang’s surprise reinstatement. History suggests we shouldn’t expect great follow-through.

Stocks I’m Watching

 

↘️ Nvidia: Concerns continue to swirl around freshly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang. His return to Nvidia sparked the best one-day market value gain on record. But the chip maker’s stock fell close to 4% premarket as investors mull multiple ongoing investigations.

 

↘️ Alibaba: A subsidiary of the Chinese tech giant was added to a U.S. blacklist intended to curb its access to American chips. Its New York-listed depositary receipts fell premarket.

 

↘️ Hewlett Packard Enterprise: The cloud-services company lifted its outlook, but the stock slid over 11% in premarket trade. Rival Dell Technologies will report after the bell.

 

↗️ Sanofi: Shares of the French drugmaker climbed after it agreed to buy U.S. peer Insmed for $41 billion. The New Jersey-based group’s stock is on track to pop too: Shares rose around 14% premarket.

 

↘️ Micron Technology, Intel, Applied Materials: After the AI trade’s rally yesterday, traders seem to be growing cautious again. Chip makers all fell premarket.
